title: Season summit: three sprints, one mountain
summary: Teach the family the next-word game, climb one peak per sprint with an old favourite waiting on each path, then write out the season's best proof and retire the monsters with honours.
materials: the season book and one fresh page for the next-word game
paper slips and a pencil each for the family tally game
graph paper for the distance climb

steps.title: The climb, in order
steps.body:
The last Think of the season, and it is a summit in the true sense: from up here you can see all twelve weeks at once.

Today has four parts, in this order: warm up the next-word game, teach it to the family, climb the season summit, then close the way mathematicians close, with the best proof written down and the monsters retired with honours.

For an encore after the next-word game, go back to the choose-2 counting problem you invented in week eleven. Bring your own group size and your own pairing action. Present it to your family, show both roads to your answer, Pascal's triangle and choices-multiply, and let them see the two ways agree. Name the ideas out loud as you explain them, not just 'I did this'.

The summit is one climb over each big idea the season built, and two old favourites wait on the path: the 21 game from sprint 1 and the threshold from sprint 2. Ten problems, no more. If one slows you down, that is the mountain doing its job. Slow on purpose beats fast and wrong on every summit in the world.

This is a challenge, never a test. Grade 6 is behind you when you reach the top, and that sentence is worth saying out loud at the table.

problems.prompt: In week 10 you played the next-word game: pick a word on a page of the season book and tally which word follows it. Say a tally page like yours showed this: after the word 'the', the page had 'day' 7 times, 'sea' 4 times and 'king' once. The game shows 'the' and asks for the best guess at the next word. Which do you pick?
explanation: The next-word game never knows the future; it bets on the tally, and the word that followed most often is the best single bet.
'Day' followed 'the' 7 times out of 12, more than 'sea' and 'king' put together.
That is the whole engine inside a chatbot: tallies from everything it has read, and a bet on a likely next word. Your paper tally is the same machine at family size.
problems.useAgain: when a guess has to come from counts of what happened before, and the biggest count is the best single bet.
hints: The game can only use the tally. Read the three counts again and let them argue.
If you had to bet one sticker on the next word, which count would you want on your side?
problems.socraticHint: What does each count on the tally actually promise about the next time 'the' shows up?

variant.prompt: Same game, another tally: after the word 'a', the page had 'wave' 2 times, 'gull' 5 times and 'boat' 3 times. The game shows 'a'. Which next word is the best guess?

problems.prompt: Keep that tally: 'the' appeared 12 times on the page, and 'day' followed it 7 of those times. Suppose the game reads on and meets 'the' 24 more times in writing that behaves like this page. About how many of those times should it expect 'day' to come next?
explanation: The page's rate is 7 out of every 12, and 24 meetings is two rounds of 12.
Two rounds of 7 is 14, so about 14 of the 24 should be 'day'.
About is the honest word: chance wobbles in small batches and calms down in long runs, so a real count of 12 or 16 would not mean the tally lied.
problems.useAgain: when a rate from a small sample sets the expectation for a longer run, and about is the only honest promise.
hints: Say the rate as a fraction first: 'day' follows 'the' 7 times out of every 12.
24 is exactly two batches of 12. What does one batch of 12 owe to 'day'?
problems.socraticHint: If the real count came out 13, would the tally be wrong, or is that just what chance does in a short run?

variant.prompt: On the same page, 'sea' followed 'the' 4 of its 12 times. In 18 more meetings with 'the' in writing like this, about how many should be 'sea'?

steps.title: Teach the family the next-word game
steps.prompt: Gather the family, the season book and a pencil each. Teach the game in one minute: pick a common word, tally what follows it on one fresh page, and the biggest count wins the bet. Then run it for ten minutes: everyone tallies a page, everyone predicts the next word at a few spots, then read on together and score the bets. Close by naming what the family just built with paper and pencil: the little engine inside every chatbot, a next-word guesser with tallies for a brain, and say in one sentence where its guesses really come from.

problems.prompt: Sprint 1 peak, the machine month: a row of five lights shows a number the week 2 way. The rightmost light is worth 1, and each light to its left is worth double the one beside it, so the leftmost is worth 2 to the power 4. The lights read on, on, off, off, on. What number is the row showing?
explanation: Build the row of values first. 2 to the power 4 is 16, then halve down the row: 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Two symbols are enough: each light is a yes or no about its own value.
Collect the yes lights: 16 and 8 from the left, then the 1 at the end.
16 plus 8 plus 1 is 25. Five little on-offs held a whole number.
problems.useAgain: when a row of on-off anythings hides a number, and adding the values of the ons reads it out.
hints: Work out 2 to the power 4 first, then halve your way down the row and write each value under its light.
Only three lights are on. Add just their three values.
problems.socraticHint: Why can no other pattern of these five lights make the same number this one makes?

variant.prompt: The same row of lights, with the leftmost still worth 2 to the power 4, changes to on, off, on, on, off. What number is it showing now?

problems.prompt: The sign for your fair table stands on the tabletop like a little tent: two straight cards leaning against each other, meeting along a top edge, feet flat on the table. The sign leans the same amount on both sides, so each card makes the same angle with the table. The two cards meet at 40 degrees at the top. How many degrees is the angle between one card and the tabletop?
explanation: The two cards and the strip of table between their feet close up into a triangle. The torn corners from week 9 proved every triangle holds 180 degrees.
The top corner takes 40 of those degrees, so 180 minus 40 leaves 140 for the two corners down on the table.
The sign leans the same amount on both sides, so those two corners are equal, and half of 140 is 70 degrees.
Check it forwards: 70 plus 70 plus 40 is 180, one straight line with no gap and no overlap.
problems.useAgain: when a leaning shape closes into a triangle with two equal corners, so the 180 total splits what is left in half.
hints: Sketch it small: two cards and the strip of table between their feet. What closed shape do the three make, and how many degrees does that shape hold?
Take the top corner's 40 out of that total. What is left belongs to two corners of exactly the same size.
problems.socraticHint: Which two of the triangle's three corners have to be equal here, and what about the sign tells you so?

variant.prompt: A second sign stands the same way, leaning the same amount on both sides, but its two cards meet at 50 degrees at the top. How many degrees is the angle between one card and the tabletop?

problems.prompt: The sprint 1 favourite, back for one more round: at the fair table a cousin challenges you to the 21 game. Take 1, 2 or 3 counters, and whoever takes the last counter wins. The pile is at 17 and it is your move. How many do you take?
explanation: The doomed piles are the multiples of 4: hand one over and the game is yours to keep.
17 sits one step above 16, the nearest multiple of 4 below it.
Take 1 and hand over 16. From then on, answer every move of theirs so your two takes make 4 together, and the last counter is yours.
problems.useAgain: when an old game comes back and the winning positions you mapped once still run it perfectly.
hints: Find the nearest multiple of 4 below 17.
Your move should hand the cousin exactly that pile.
problems.socraticHint: If you hand the cousin a multiple of 4 now, what can you always do after every move they make?

variant.prompt: The rematch starts from a pile of 19, your move. How many counters do you take?

problems.prompt: Sprint 2 peak, the balance month: wrapping the gift needs more than 70 cm of ribbon to go all the way around with a bow. The roll started at 110 cm, some went to the board trim, and the leftover r fits the equation r + 35 = 110. True or false: the leftover ribbon is enough for the wrap.
explanation: Settle the equation first: take 35 off both sides, and r is 110 minus 35, which is 75 cm.
Now the rule: the wrap needs more than 70, and 75 is more than 70.
True, with 5 cm to spare. The equation pins down the one exact number; the inequality then judges whether it makes the cut.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains an equation that finds the number with an inequality that judges it.
hints: Two sentences hide in here: one tells you exactly how much ribbon is left, the other sets the bar. Solve the exact one first.
Once you know r, read the rule slowly: more than 70 means 70 itself would not have been enough.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two sentences could you check with a ruler, and which one needed algebra before you could check anything?

variant.prompt: Another roll: the leftover s fits the equation s + 28 = 96, and the wrap still needs more than 70 cm. True or false: this leftover is enough.

problems.prompt: Your fair table hands out thank-you packs: 36 photo cards and 48 stickers, every pack identical, nothing left over. What is the biggest number of packs you can make?
explanation: Identical packs with nothing left over means the number of packs must divide 36 and divide 48 both, and the biggest number that divides both is the gcd.
Euclid's shrinking game from week 6, replacing the bigger number each time: 48 and 36 becomes 12 and 36, then 12 and 24.
Next comes a tie at 12 and 12, and a tie is where the game stops, so the gcd is 12.
Twelve packs, each holding 3 photo cards and 4 stickers. Check it forwards: 12 x 3 is 36 and 12 x 4 is 48.
problems.useAgain: when two amounts must split into identical groups with nothing left, and the biggest shared divisor sets the group count.
hints: Every pack gets the same share of each pile, so the pack count must divide both 36 and 48.
Play the week 6 subtraction game with 36 and 48 and see where it stops.
problems.socraticHint: Why must the number of packs divide both piles, not just one of them?

variant.prompt: A smaller table: 30 photo cards and 42 stickers, identical packs, nothing left over. What is the biggest number of packs?

problems.prompt: The paper backing for your fair table sign is drawn on graph paper as a house shape: a rectangle 10 squares across and 6 squares tall, with a triangle roof standing on the rectangle's whole top edge. The roof's peak sits 4 squares above that edge, directly above its middle. How many grid squares of paper does the whole sign take?
explanation: Area in pieces: the sign is a rectangle with a triangle sitting on top, and both pieces are shapes you already know.
The rectangle holds 10 x 6, which is 60 grid squares.
Cut the roof straight down from its peak and you get two right triangles, each with legs of 5 and 4 squares. Each one is half of a 5 by 4 rectangle, so it holds 10, and the roof holds 20 in all.
60 plus 20 is 80 grid squares.
The other chop agrees. Box the whole sign inside a 10 by 10 square, which holds 100 grid squares. Take away the two empty corner triangles above the roof, 10 squares each, and 100 take 20 leaves 80.
problems.useAgain: when a shape is a rectangle with a triangle on top, so chopping it into pieces you know, or boxing it and taking the empty corners off, both count the same area.
hints: Draw it on graph paper first. Count the rectangle's squares before you touch the roof.
Cut the roof straight down from its peak. Each half is a right triangle, and a right triangle is half of the rectangle you can draw around it.
problems.socraticHint: The peak sits directly above the middle of the top edge. What does that let you say about the roof's two halves?

variant.prompt: A smaller sign, the same house shape: the rectangle is 8 squares across and 5 squares tall, and the roof's peak sits 3 squares above the top edge, directly above its middle. How many grid squares of paper does it take?

problems.prompt: The sprint 2 favourite, back on duty: the creature guards your fair table, telling day from evening with its light sensor. You set its fence at 54, dead halfway between the two crowds, and the dim crowd sits around 32. Where does the bright crowd sit?
explanation: Halfway means the fence keeps the same distance from each crowd, so measure the side you already know.
From the dim crowd at 32 up to the fence at 54 is 22 steps, so the bright crowd sits 22 steps past 54.
54 plus 22 is 76. Run the week 6 recipe forwards to check: 32 and 76 add to 108, and half of 108 is 54.
problems.useAgain: when a halfway number and one of its two neighbours are known and the missing neighbour sits the same distance out the other side.
hints: The fence is the same distance from the dim crowd as from the bright one. Which of those two distances can you already count?
Count the steps from 32 up to 54, then walk that many steps on past 54.
problems.socraticHint: If someone nudged the fence to 60 without touching the sensor, which crowd would start getting called by the wrong name?

variant.prompt: Back home that evening you set the fence at 47 and the bright crowd sits around 68. Where does the dim crowd sit?

problems.prompt: Sprint 3 peak, the counting month: you roll two dice at the fair table. Which is the better bet, a sum of 7 or a sum of 12?
explanation: Choices multiply: 6 faces on the first die and 6 on the second make 6 x 6, which is 36 equally likely rolls.
A sum of 12 happens one way only: 6 with 6. A sum of 7 happens six ways: 1 with 6, 2 with 5, 3 with 4, 4 with 3, 5 with 2 and 6 with 1.
Six ways beat one way, so 7 is the better bet, six times over. Counting the ways is the whole trick.
problems.useAgain: when two outcomes look like fair rivals and counting the ways to each settles the bet.
hints: First count every roll two dice can make, first die then second die.
Now list every pair that sums to 12, then every pair that sums to 7. Keep 2 with 5 and 5 with 2 as different rolls.
problems.socraticHint: Why does 3 with 4 count separately from 4 with 3, when both show the same two faces on the table?

variant.prompt: Same table, new bet: a sum of 10 or a sum of 2. Which is the better bet?

problems.prompt: Two readings on a sensor plot like your week 11 one sit at the points (-2, -1) and (2, 2) on graph paper. Use the squares trick from week 11: how far apart are the two points, in grid units, measured straight along the slanted line between them?
explanation: The two points make a right triangle: from -2 across to 2 is 4 steps, and from -1 up to 2 is 3 steps.
Square on the side: the squares on the two straight sides hold 4 x 4 and 3 x 3, which is 16 plus 9, so the square on the slanted side holds 25.
A square of area 25 has side 5, so the points sit exactly 5 units apart. That is the exact ruler nearest-neighbour reaches for.
problems.useAgain: when two points on a plot need an exact distance and the squares on the two straight sides pay for the slanted one.
hints: Count the across step and the up step between the two points first; crossing zero does not change how many steps it is.
The big square's area is the two small squares added together. What side length gives that area?
problems.socraticHint: Why is the slanted distance not just the across step plus the up step, the way a taxi would drive it?

variant.prompt: Two more points sit at (-3, -2) and (3, 6). How far apart are they, in grid units, measured straight along the slanted line between them?

problems.prompt: The last step of the climb: a little keepsake box from the fair table measures 2 1/2 cm by 2 cm by 1 1/2 cm. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
explanation: Volume multiplies the three edges, and of means times works for fractions too: 5/2 x 2 x 3/2.
5/2 x 2 is 5, and 5 x 3/2 is 15/2, which is 7 1/2 cubic centimeters.
The cube check agrees: half-centimeter cubes fill the box 5 by 4 by 3, which is 60 little cubes, and 8 of them make one cubic centimeter, so 60 divided by 8 is 7 1/2 again.
problems.useAgain: when a box has fractional edges and multiplying them, or packing it with smaller cubes, gives the same volume twice.
hints: Write each edge as a fraction: 5/2, 2 and 3/2, then multiply them in any order you like.
Pair the easy two first: what is 5/2 x 2?
problems.socraticHint: Whole-number boxes get checked by counting unit cubes. What size of cube would let you count this one out?

variant.prompt: A longer keepsake box measures 3 1/2 cm by 2 cm by 1 1/2 cm. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?

steps.title: Explain it: the best proof, and the monsters retired
steps.prompt: Write the season's best proof for a friend who was never at your table and cannot stop you to ask a question. Choose the 21 game's domino argument, the hundred lockers' divisor pairs or Nim's binary balance, and set it down one idea per sentence: the first step, the step that repeats, and the last sentence that closes it. Add one sentence on why this proof beat the other two, because on paper the reason has to stand up without your voice behind it. Then rule a line under it and retire the season's monsters with honours in writing: the 1-2-4 game, the hundred lockers and the squares on the chessboard, one line each naming the move that cracked it. Read the page back once and cut any sentence that only works with you sitting beside the reader, because what is left goes in the season book for next season's you to read.
